name: Irish Dance
notes: Irish Dance style pack (Doc 04 template, foundation-forward). Three living branches told honestly: competitive solo step dance (the Riverdance style — codified by An Coimisiún and the schools, learned with certified teachers), céilí social dancing (group figures, walkable by any beginner at a céilí night), and sean-nós (the older, low-to-the-ground, improvisational style from the Gaeltacht — looser arms, battering steps, danced on a door taken off its hinges in the lore). Riverdance (1994, a Eurovision interval act that conquered the planet) is credited as the moment that made this dance global — Bill Whelan's score, Michael Flatley and Jean Butler leading. Design truths: the soft-shoe basics (point, hop, the 1-2-3s, skip-2-3s) are genuinely solo-trainable and build extraordinary ankle spring; posture is curriculum (tall carriage, arms low — a convention whose origin stories are lore, told as lore); competitive technique beyond basics is teacher-taught, stated honestly; the céilí is the social door anyone can walk through tonight.

seasons.finale: Film yourself lilting or clapping a reel's rhythm through one full tune — the ear before the feet.
Film the 1-2-3s traveling and turning — light, lifted, landing like rain.
Film skip-2-3s and side-7s across the room — posture tall, arms easy, spring alive.
Film 30 seconds of low, loose, improvised battering to a reel — the older style's freedom, honestly attempted.
Find a céilí night — the caller teaches every figure, and beginners have always been the point.

attributes.name: Ankle spring L1
attributes.test: 90s of light continuous bounce on the balls of the feet, heels never slamming, calves pain-free

attributes.name: Ankle spring L2
attributes.test: 30 relaxed single-foot hops each side, landing quiet and lifted — Irish dance is rain, not thunder

attributes.name: Carriage L1
attributes.test: 60s of bouncing with a tall spine and still, easy arms — no shoulder creep, no forward lean

nodes.name: Reels, jigs, hornpipes — the tune families
checkpoints: reels run in 4/4 (the workhorse), jigs in 6/8, hornpipes swagger in swung 4/4 — each has its own steps
learn to LILT: singing the rhythm ('diddly-dee') is how this tradition has always taught it
the tune phrases in 8-bar parts, usually AABB — your steps phrase with them

nodes.name: The lift — dancing on top of the beat
checkpoints: Irish dance rides slightly on top of the beat — buoyant, never dragging
the music's 'lift' and the dancer's spring are the same thing in two bodies
session musicians will tell you when you have it; until then, your landings will (quiet = yes)

nodes.name: Three branches: step, céilí, sean-nós
checkpoints: competitive step dance: the upright, precise solo form the world knows — codified by An Coimisiún and the schools, learned with certified teachers
céilí dancing: social group figures, called and taught in the room — the door anyone can walk through
sean-nós: the older Gaeltacht style — low, loose-armed, improvised, danced small (on a door taken off its hinges, in the lore)
one tradition, three temperaments; this pack preps you for all three doors

nodes.name: 1994 — the Riverdance moment
checkpoints: a seven-minute Eurovision interval act (1994) — Bill Whelan's score, Michael Flatley and Jean Butler leading — turned Irish dance into a global phenomenon overnight
the arms-low convention predates the show; its origin stories (clergy, crowded cottages, defiance) are LORE — enjoy them as lore, dance the posture as technique
every Irish dance school on earth felt 1994; if you're here, so did you

nodes.name: Points & hops
checkpoints: point the toe to the front — turned out, arched, weightless; hop on the standing foot, landing soft
posture is half the step: tall spine, arms easy at the sides, chin level
the hop lands THROUGH the foot — toe, ball, whisper of heel
mistakes: landing flat and loud (Irish dance is rain, not thunder)
shoulders creeping up to help the hop

nodes.name: The 1-2-3s (promenade step)
nodes.anchor: the step under half of Irish dancing
checkpoints: hop, then three light steps — hop-1-2-3, alternating lead feet
travel forward, backward, and in a turn — same step, every direction
on the balls of the feet the whole time; the heels are for special occasions
lilt it as you dance it: 'hop-one-two-three' until the mouth and feet agree
mistakes: three even stomps with no hop lift
watching the floor (the floor has never once moved)

nodes.name: Side-7s & skip-2-3s
checkpoints: side-7: seven quick lateral counts, crossing light, traveling clean — céilí dancing's highway
skip-2-3s string 1-2-3s into flowing travel
these two plus the 1-2-3s are enough to survive any céilí figure a caller throws at you

nodes.name: The rising step (light jig, 6/8)
checkpoints: jig time is 6/8 — lilt it as 'rashers-and-sausages' like generations before you
hop, hop-back, hop-back — the rising step lifts twice and settles, riding the jig's two big pulses
same rain-quiet landings; the tune changed, the manners didn't
mistakes: dancing reel rhythm over a jig (the tune will fight you and win)

nodes.name: Sean-nós battering (intro)
nodes.origin: the older Gaeltacht tradition — low, close to the floor, improvised; the ancestor the stage style stands on
checkpoints: drop the formality: knees soft, arms loose, steps small and close to the floor
batter the rhythm — heel and toe strikes improvised inside the reel, more tap-cousin than stage-Irish
dance it in a one-metre square; the old style was danced small on purpose
this is an introduction; the Gaeltacht's living tradition is the real teacher
mistakes: doing stage steps with loose arms and calling it sean-nós — the whole engine is different

nodes.name: A full step to a reel — filmed
checkpoints: compose one 8-bar step from your vocabulary (1-2-3s, points, side-7s) and dance it through both parts of a reel
landings quiet, posture tall, lift audible in the silence between sounds
competitive technique beyond this lives with certified teachers — stated honestly; the céilí needs no certificate at all

nodes.name: The céilí night
checkpoints: find a céilí — Irish cultural centers and pubs run them worldwide, and the caller teaches every figure in the room
the Walls of Limerick or the Siege of Ennis will be called; your side-7s and 1-2-3s are the whole entry fee
stay for the session music after; the tunes are the tradition's beating heart
